title: Dunlop v. Bachowski (1975)
summary: The Secretary of Labor's decision not to sue to set aside a union election is judicially reviewable, but review is confined to a statement of reasons and asks only whether that statement shows the decision to be so irrational as to be arbitrary and capricious.
notes:
Key line: "For a statement of reasons must be adequate to enable the court to determine whether the Secretary's decision was reached for an impermissible reason or for no reason at all." (Brennan, J.)

Citation: 421 U.S. 560 (1975).

sections.Parties: The petitioner was John T. Dunlop, Secretary of Labor, substituted for his predecessor Peter J. Brennan, who had declined to bring a civil action to set aside a union election. The respondent was Walter Bachowski, a member of the United Steelworkers of America who had lost the February 13, 1973, election for Director of District 20 to the incumbent, Kay Kluz, by 10,558 votes to 9,651, with a third candidate receiving 3,566. The United Steelworkers of America, AFL-CIO, was also a respondent. The United Mine Workers and the Association for Union Democracy filed amicus briefs urging affirmance of the decision below.
sections.Material Facts: Title IV of the Labor Management Reporting and Disclosure Act of 1959, 29 U.S.C. section 482, lets a union member who has exhausted internal remedies complain to the Secretary of Labor about an election, requires the Secretary to investigate, and provides that if he finds probable cause to believe a violation occurred and has not been remedied he shall sue within sixty days to set aside the election. After exhausting his remedies within the union, Bachowski filed a timely complaint alleging violations of section 401 in the District 20 election. The Department investigated 80 of the district's 190 local unions. By letter dated November 7, 1973, the Secretary told Bachowski that civil action to set aside the election was not warranted, without stating reasons. A statement of reasons filed after remand, and appended to the Court's opinion, found violations in seventeen locals that could theoretically have affected at most 884 votes, fewer than Kluz's 907 vote margin.
sections.Procedural History: On November 7, 1973, Bachowski sued the Secretary and the union in the United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania, asking the court to declare the Secretary's refusal arbitrary and capricious and to order him to file suit. After a hearing the district court dismissed on November 12, 1973, concluding it lacked authority to grant the relief. The Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit reversed, 502 F.2d 79 (1974), holding that the court had jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. section 1337, that the decision was reviewable under the APA, and that Bachowski was entitled to a specific statement of the factors the Secretary relied on and to challenge the factual basis of the decision. The Supreme Court granted certiorari, 419 U.S. 1068 (1974), and on June 2, 1975, reversed in part and directed proceedings on remand consistent with its opinion.
sections.Issue: Whether the Secretary of Labor's decision not to bring a civil action under Title IV of the LMRDA to set aside a union election is subject to judicial review at all, or is precluded by statute or committed to agency discretion within 5 U.S.C. section 701(a); and, if the decision is reviewable under the arbitrary and capricious standard of section 706(2)(A), how far that review may extend, in particular whether the complaining member may obtain a trial type inquiry into the factual basis of the Secretary's conclusion that no violation affected the election's outcome.
sections.Holding: The Court held that the district court had jurisdiction under section 1337 and that the Secretary's decision not to sue is reviewable, because the LMRDA contains no express prohibition and the Secretary failed to carry the heavy burden of showing by clear and convincing evidence that Congress meant to preclude review. But it held that the scope of review must be narrowly limited to serve the statute's objectives. The Secretary must furnish the court and the complaining member a statement of reasons, and the court's review is confined to examining that statement to determine whether, without more, it shows the decision to be so irrational as to be arbitrary and capricious. The Third Circuit erred insofar as it authorized a trial type inquiry into the factual bases of the Secretary's conclusions.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Brennan relied on Abbott Laboratories v. Gardner for the presumption of reviewability and found not the slightest intimation that Congress had thought about precluding review. He then drew on Calhoon v. Harvey, Wirtz v. Bottle Blowers Association and Trbovich v. Mine Workers to identify Congress's purposes: to use the Secretary's special knowledge and discretion, to protect unions from frivolous litigation, to settle quickly the cloud on incumbents' titles, and to centralize litigation in a single proceeding. Because the statute relies on the Secretary's discretion to determine both the probable violation and its probable effect on the outcome, a court may not substitute its judgment for his. To permit intelligent review, however, the Secretary must supply a statement of reasons informing the court and the member of the grounds of decision and the essential facts on which his inferences rest; a reasons requirement also promotes careful thought and serves the member for whom the Secretary in effect acts as lawyer. The full trappings of an adversary trial would defeat Congress's aim of avoiding delay. The November 7 letter might satisfy the brief statement requirement of APA section 555(e) but not the LMRDA. Only in rare cases, such as a declared refusal to enforce Title IV, might review go beyond the statement. If the statement shows the decision rational the suit must be dismissed, and the Court reserved whether a court could ever order the Secretary to sue.

topics.lrs-n-nonreviewability: Mandatory enforcement criteria supplied law to apply despite the general concern for prosecutorial discretion.

learning.separateOpinions: Chief Justice Burger concurred, stressing that the Court had fashioned an exceedingly narrow scope of review and that the Secretary's decision may be held arbitrary and capricious only where his own statement of reasons shows irregularities that affected the outcome and he nevertheless refuses to sue without a rational reason. Justice Rehnquist concurred in the result in part and dissented in part. He objected that the Court decided the statement of reasons issue, which the parties no longer disputed and which was not in the question presented, while reserving the question actually presented, whether a court may compel the Secretary to sue, and he found the Court's reasoning convoluted because a reasons requirement made sense only if a court could ultimately order suit.
